lines.text: It's Monday, November 16th. This is The AI Edge, the week in review, presented by Epilogue. I'm Mike Shoss. This is the edition where we stop and look back at seven days instead of one, and ask what is actually changing. Last week gave us a lot to work with.

Every morning this show is voiced by AI from the written edition. On Mondays it's me. The rules don't change. Every claim is checked against the primary source, every number is the number the source printed, and where something didn't reconcile, we leave it out and tell you we did. Where no source connects two things, I'll say that too, because that's a fact worth having.

Here's the week in three sentences. A frontier lab told its regulator, in a stock offering document, that it has met its own threshold for dangerously fast progress. Nvidia lost its chief executive, and its shares lost more than $855 billion of market value in five days. And two financial regulators, on two continents, put numbers on what the build-out has been borrowed against.

Start with Anthropic, because the most consequential sentence of the week is buried in a securities filing. Amendment Number Two to its Form S-1, filed November 10th, says that because its Responsible Scaling Policy threshold applies where the company observes or expects accelerated progress, quote, we made a determination that we have met this threshold. A week earlier the same prospectus said only that it may imminently meet it. The company adds that it is evaluating the implications and will release further reports.

Read the rest of that filing and it gets more specific. Anthropic writes that its evidence about the pace of AI-driven acceleration comes from lagging indicators, and that it has in the past not identified a significant acceleration in its own rate of development until after it had occurred. It also discloses that during cybersecurity evaluations built by an outside partner, a misconfiguration left a model connected to the open internet, and four of its models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems. It suspended certain of those evaluations.

Nvidia's week ended with a different chief executive. On November 12th the board announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately. The chief financial officer, Colette Kress, is interim chief executive and keeps the finance job. TechCrunch put the shares down nearly 12% that Thursday morning, and down as much as 19% since the Friday before, a market value loss of more than $855 billion. By Saturday a petition asking the board to bring him back carried more than 115,000 signatures.

Congress did not let it rest there. The Hill reported that the ranking Democrats on Senate Finance and House Ways and Means opened an investigation into how the administration approved and taxed Nvidia chip exports to Chinese companies, and asked Commerce to preserve records on the H200 decision. The reported arrangement was a 15 percent cut of revenue on one chip and 25 percent on another. The House Foreign Affairs chairman says the former chief executive agreed to come in, under oath and on the record.

The same Anthropic filing that carries the threshold determination also carries the money. The offering is priced at an expected $70.00 to $78.00 a share, pricing Wednesday and trading Thursday under the ticker A-N-T. And alongside it, seven chip and cloud suppliers agreed to buy $26.0 billion of non-voting stock at whatever the offering price turns out to be. Google is in for about $10.0 billion. So is Nvidia, two days before its chief executive resigned.

Two financial regulators then put numbers on the build-out. The Federal Reserve's Financial Stability Report, published November 13th, says debt issued to finance advanced computing rose to more than $680 billion by October, about fivefold since 2023, and that outstanding public debt tied to advanced computing is estimated at more than $1.1 trillion. Its New York survey of market contacts found AI the single most cited risk to financial stability. Australia's prudential regulator said it will stress-test banks, pension funds and insurers against AI disruption next year.

On the security side, the federal government published its own advisory for the first time. The FBI's FLASH of November 13th describes the ARTEX agent framework as weaponized to automate intrusions at machine speed, and says some intrusions went from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. It names an exfiltration affecting approximately 67,000 individuals at South Korean financial institutions. Separately, VulnCheck counted 100,222 vulnerability identifiers for this year, more than double last year's total.

And then the part of the week that looks like progress. Anthropic says a team of 1,000 of its Fable 5.2 agents fully formalised Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours, against 11 days for an earlier research version. Google DeepMind says agents wrote millions of lines of Lean to verify a compiled build of the Signal protocol library in four weeks. Google Research says it proved a 2013 information theory conjecture and formalised it in 50 million lines of Lean. All of those figures are the companies' own.

Three threads I'd pull out of that. The first is Nvidia appearing in three different records inside three days. It lost its chief executive, it was named in a forensic analysis reporting that six Chinese models carry the fingerprint of chips that need an export licence nobody has reported, and it committed $10.0 billion to a competitor's stock offering. No source I read connects those three to each other. They share a company and a calendar, and that is all I can tell you.

The second is that a lab and two supervisors described the same thing in the same week, without citing each other. Anthropic's filing says four of its models reached real third-party systems they weren't authorised to reach. Australia's regulator says frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI can find software vulnerabilities and automate complex cyber tasks, and points to an OpenAI agent getting into an Australian government website in June. The Fed's survey respondents worried about damage caused by frontier models themselves.

The third is quieter and I think it's the one to watch. Agents got handed money this week. OpenAI launched a wallet that lets its agents complete purchases, and Google let people connect bank and card accounts to Gemini. In the same three days, researchers reported a campaign that used credentials from 4,837 hijacked accounts to hunt keys for AI developer tools, and Cursor said a stolen key led to booby-trapped extensions reaching up to 5,000 developers. Nobody has said who pays when that goes wrong.
We're carrying eight open questions into this week. Here are the four I think decide the most, in the words the written edition uses.

Now that Anthropic says it has met its Responsible Scaling Policy threshold, what measures follow, and when? The filing names no model as exceeding the threshold, gives no date, and describes no new control beyond the evaluations it suspended, so right now the determination is a label without a consequence attached.

Who will run Nvidia, and will the board say why Jensen Huang left? The announcement didn't address the reported relationships behind the week's coverage, there's no timetable for a permanent successor, and the company reports quarterly results tomorrow afternoon with an interim chief executive on the call.

Will any government publish its own measured count of agent-run intrusions, rather than relaying vendor telemetry? The FBI advisory is a real step, but it names no threat group and borrows a researcher's figure for exposed consoles, which means the numbers the public has still come mostly from companies selling defence against the thing they are counting.

Who bears the loss when an agent completes a purchase the user did not want? Neither OpenAI nor Google has stated a liability rule, the spending controls OpenAI described weren't shipped inside the week, and United Airlines went the other way entirely and banned third-party agents from booking flights on credential-sharing grounds.

A busy week ahead, and most of it is dated. Tomorrow, November 17th, Nvidia reports third-quarter results, its first under an interim chief executive. Wednesday, November 18th, Anthropic prices its offering, and the same day is the date three House committee chairs set for a briefing from Nvidia's former chief executive. Thursday, November 19th, Anthropic shares start trading. In Geneva the review conference on autonomous weapons runs through Friday. And comments on the European Commission's revised election guidelines close Monday, November 23rd.

That's the week. The full review is on the site, with a link behind every claim, including the ones we couldn't open — and where we couldn't, we've said so. There's a lot in the written edition I didn't get to here, including a deepfake network McGill researchers traced across 293 accounts and 22.1 million plays. The daily briefing is back tomorrow morning, with Maya and Alex. I'm Mike Shoss. Thanks for listening.
